music.title: Feeling the Blues
music.description: Find the rhythm. Hear the pattern. Make it your own.
notes: The roots of blues
Blues developed in African American communities in the United States. Its lyrics express experiences and feelings. Your unit explores its history, social context, musical features, and performance.
Feel the backbeat
In common 4/4 blues grooves, the backbeat emphasizes beats 2 and 4. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” steadily, then clap on 2 and 4.
The 12-bar pattern
A common 12-bar blues uses the I, IV, and V chords over twelve bars. One basic version is I–I–I–I / IV–IV–I–I / V–IV–I–I. Other versions use variations.
Blues lyrics
An AAB verse repeats its first line, then answers or develops it with a different third line. For your lyric-writing assessment, follow the instructions and table in your class worksheets.

maths.description: Small steps through some powerful numbers.
notes: Types of numbers
Integers are whole numbers, including negatives and zero. A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers with a non-zero denominator.
Rational or irrational?
Terminating and recurring decimals are rational. Irrational numbers, such as √2 and π, cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers.
Roots & powers
Squaring means multiplying a number by itself. The principal square root reverses squaring and is non-negative. For example, √81 = 9 and ∛27 = 3.
BIDMAS & indices
Calculate brackets, then indices, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. For the same base, aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ.

notes: What is a network?
A computer network connects devices so they can exchange data and share resources, such as printers or files.
LANs & WANs
A LAN covers a limited area, such as a school building. A WAN connects across much larger areas and can connect multiple LANs.
Network devices
A switch connects devices within a network. A router forwards data between networks. A wireless access point lets devices join a network using Wi-Fi.
Staying secure
Use unique passwords and multi-factor authentication. Be cautious with unexpected links, keep software updated, and never share your password.

science.name: Science
science.title: Think like a scientist
science.description: Ask questions, test ideas, and follow the evidence.
notes: Ask a question
A testable scientific question can be investigated through observations or measurements. A prediction describes what you expect to happen.
Plan an investigation
Plan what you will change, measure, and keep the same. Repeat measurements and follow your teacher’s laboratory safety instructions.
Choose your variables
The independent variable is what you change. The dependent variable is what you measure. Control variables are kept the same to make comparisons fair.
Read the evidence
Look for patterns, unusual results, and limits in your data. Support your conclusion with evidence, and explain whether the results support your prediction.

german.description: Read, discuss, and bring a modern drama to life.
notes: Ein Drama lesen
Ein Drama ist für die Aufführung geschrieben. Dialoge und Regieanweisungen zeigen, was Figuren sagen und wie eine Szene gestaltet werden kann.
Figuren verstehen
Untersuche, was eine Figur sagt und tut. Begründe Aussagen über ihre Eigenschaften mit passenden Textstellen.
Dialog & Wirkung
Wortwahl, Pausen und Sprechweise können Beziehungen und Konflikte deutlich machen. Achte darauf, wie Figuren aufeinander reagieren.
Redewiedergabe
Direkte Rede gibt Worte unmittelbar wieder, meist mit Anführungszeichen. Indirekte Rede berichtet über das Gesagte; in formellen Texten wird dafür oft Konjunktiv I verwendet.

notes: Population patterns
Population distribution describes where people live. Physical and human factors can influence whether an area is densely or sparsely populated.
Population density
Population density is the number of people per unit of area. Divide the total population by the area, using consistent units.
Births & deaths
Natural increase is births minus deaths over a period. Migration also changes population size, so total population change includes both.
Population pyramids & migration
A population pyramid displays age and sex structure. Migration is movement to live in another place. Push factors encourage people to leave; pull factors attract them elsewhere.

art.name: Art
art.title: The principles of design
art.description: Explore how balance, rhythm, and contrast bring an artwork together.
notes: Emphasis & contrast
Emphasis draws attention to an important part of an artwork. Contrast places noticeably different elements together—for example, light beside dark—to create visual interest.
Balance & movement
Balance distributes visual weight across an image. It can be symmetrical, asymmetrical, or radial. Movement guides the viewer’s eye through a composition.
Pattern & rhythm
Pattern repeats an element or arrangement. Rhythm uses repetition and variation to create a visual beat and guide the eye.
Unity & proportion

Unity helps separate parts of an artwork feel connected. Proportion describes how the sizes of parts relate to one another. For the A3 project, explain the principles you have chosen and how they communicate your idea.

number.title: Number, percentages & proportionality
number.concept: A percentage expresses a quantity per hundred. A percentage change uses the original quantity as its denominator. Ratio compares quantities using a shared scale; direct proportion means one quantity is a constant multiple of the other.
number.example: A price of €80 rises by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = €92. A later 15% decrease gives 92 × 0.85 = €78.20, so equal percentage increases and decreases do not cancel.
number.q: A €60 item is reduced by 20%. What is the new price?
number.why: Twenty percent of 60 is 12. Subtract 12 from the original 60.

algebra.title: Algebra & equations
algebra.concept: An equation is a balance: applying the same valid operation to both sides preserves equality. Expand brackets before collecting like terms. When multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.
algebra.example: Solve 3(x − 2) = 15: divide by 3 to obtain x − 2 = 5, then add 2 to obtain x = 7. Substitution into the original equation checks the result.
algebra.why: Subtract 7 to get 2x = 12; divide by 2 to get x = 6.

quadratics.title: Quadratics & completing the square
quadratics.concept: A quadratic contains a non-zero x² term. Factoring, completing the square, and the quadratic formula offer different routes to its roots. Vertex form a(x − h)² + k makes the turning point (h, k) visible.
quadratics.example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4. The vertex is (−3, −4), and the roots are −1 and −5.
quadratics.q: What is the vertex of y = (x − 2)² + 3?
quadratics.why: In vertex form, h = 2 and k = 3. The square is zero when x = 2.

functions.title: Functions & transformations
functions.concept: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. f(x) + k shifts a graph vertically, while f(x − h) shifts it right by h. An inverse reverses a one-to-one mapping; restricting the domain may be necessary.
functions.example: For f(x) = 2x + 3, write y = 2x + 3 and rearrange to x = (y − 3)/2. Thus f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.
functions.q: What does y = f(x − 4) do to the graph of y = f(x)?
functions.why: The same output now occurs when the input is 4 larger.

geometry.title: Geometry & similarity
geometry.concept: Congruent shapes have equal corresponding sides and angles. Similar shapes preserve angles and have a constant scale factor for corresponding lengths. Areas scale with the square of that factor; volumes scale with its cube.
geometry.example: A similar solid is enlarged by a length factor of 3. Its surface area becomes 9 times as large and its volume becomes 27 times as large.
geometry.q: A rectangle is enlarged by factor 2.5. Its area is multiplied by…
geometry.why: Area uses two dimensions, so the factor is 2.5² = 6.25.

trigonometry.title: Trigonometry
trigonometry.concept: In a right triangle, sine, cosine, and tangent compare pairs of sides relative to an angle. Always identify the hypotenuse first and check whether your calculator uses degrees or radians. The sine and cosine rules extend calculations to non-right triangles.
trigonometry.example: If the hypotenuse is 10 cm and an angle is 30°, the opposite side is 10 sin 30° = 5 cm.
trigonometry.q: Which ratio equals tan θ in a right triangle?
trigonometry.why: Tangent compares the opposite side with the adjacent side.

statistics.title: Statistics & data interpretation
statistics.concept: The mean uses every value and can be influenced by extreme observations. The median is the middle of ordered data. Spread describes variability; always consider the sample and collection method before drawing conclusions about a population.
statistics.example: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, the mean is 6 but the median is 3. The unusually large observation pulls the mean upward.
statistics.q: Which summary is usually less affected by a single extreme outlier?
statistics.why: The median depends on position in the ordered data, not the size of an extreme value.

probability.title: Probability & conditional reasoning
probability.concept: For independent events, multiply probabilities to find the probability of both. For mutually exclusive events, add probabilities to find the probability of either. Conditional probability restricts attention to outcomes where the condition holds.
probability.example: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Without replacement, P(two red) = (3/5)(2/4) = 3/10. The second probability changes after the first draw.
probability.q: A fair coin is tossed twice. What is P(two heads)?
probability.why: The independent outcomes each have probability 1/2, giving 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

differentiation.title: Differentiation & rates of change
differentiation.concept: A derivative measures an instantaneous rate of change and gives the gradient of a tangent. For a power xⁿ, the derivative is nxⁿ⁻¹. Stationary points satisfy f′(x) = 0, but additional analysis determines whether they are maxima, minima, or neither.
differentiation.example: If s(t) = t³ − 3t, velocity is v(t) = 3t² − 3. At t = 2, the velocity is 9 distance units per time unit.
differentiation.why: Apply the power rule: multiply by 3 and lower the power by 1.

integration.title: Integration & accumulation
integration.concept: An indefinite integral gives a family of antiderivatives, so include an arbitrary constant. A definite integral measures signed accumulation over an interval. Area below the horizontal axis contributes negatively to a signed integral.
integration.example: ∫₂⁴ 3x² dx = [x³]₂⁴ = 64 − 8 = 56. Evaluate at the upper limit, then subtract the value at the lower limit.
integration.why: Differentiating x² gives 2x; the constant disappears under differentiation.

sequences.title: Sequences, series & financial models
sequences.concept: An arithmetic sequence adds a constant difference; a geometric sequence multiplies by a constant ratio. Compound growth is geometric when the percentage rate is fixed. A model should state assumptions about rates and the time period.
sequences.example: €500 growing by 4% each year becomes 500(1.04)³ after three years. Do not round intermediate values unnecessarily.
sequences.why: Each term is twice the previous one. The common ratio is 2.

vectors.title: Vectors & mathematical modelling
vectors.concept: A vector has magnitude and direction. Add vectors by adding corresponding components. The scalar product links algebraic components with the angle between vectors and can test perpendicularity.
vectors.why: Their dot product is 1×2 + 2×(−1) = 0, so they are perpendicular.

complex.title: Complex numbers & proof
complex.concept: Complex numbers extend real numbers by introducing i, with i² = −1. Algebraic and polar forms describe the same number. Mathematical proof establishes a claim for all allowed cases rather than checking only a few examples.
complex.example: (2 + i)(2 − i) = 4 − i² = 5. Multiplying conjugates produces a real number.

modelling.title: Regression & evaluating models
modelling.concept: A mathematical model simplifies a real situation using assumptions. Regression describes an association in observed data; it does not establish a causal mechanism. Predictions far outside the data range are especially uncertain.
modelling.example: A line fitted to study times between 1 and 8 hours should not automatically be trusted to predict a result for 60 hours. The relationship may stop being linear.
modelling.q: Predicting beyond the observed data range is called…
modelling.why: Extrapolation extends a model outside the range in which it was fitted.

cells.title: Cells & membrane transport
cells.concept: Cells are the basic units of living organisms. The cell membrane regulates movement of substances. Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient; active transport uses energy to move substances against such a gradient.
cells.example: Oxygen can diffuse into a respiring cell when its concentration is higher outside. A root hair cell may use active transport to absorb mineral ions against a gradient.
cells.q: Which process requires an energy supply to move substances against a concentration gradient?
cells.why: Active transport uses energy, often supplied by ATP.

enzymes.title: Enzymes & biological reactions
enzymes.concept: Enzymes catalyse reactions by lowering activation energy. Their active sites interact with particular substrates. Temperature and pH can change activity; sufficiently disruptive conditions alter protein structure and reduce function.
enzymes.example: Heating an enzyme initially increases collision frequency. Above an appropriate range, structural changes reduce the number of functional active sites.
enzymes.q: Why can very high temperatures reduce enzyme activity?
options: The active site can change shape
enzymes.why: Denaturation can change the active site so the substrate no longer binds effectively.

photosynthesis.title: Photosynthesis & respiration
photosynthesis.concept: Photosynthesis transfers light energy into chemical stores, using carbon dioxide and water to build carbohydrates. Aerobic respiration releases usable energy from organic molecules using oxygen. Plants respire as well as photosynthesise.
photosynthesis.example: A plant kept in darkness cannot sustain photosynthesis, but living cells continue to respire using stored compounds while supplies last.
photosynthesis.q: Most of the carbon in a plant’s newly made glucose comes from…
photosynthesis.why: Carbon dioxide supplies carbon atoms. Light provides energy rather than matter.

genetics.title: Inheritance, DNA & variation
genetics.concept: DNA stores genetic information in a sequence of bases. Alleles are alternative versions of a gene. An organism’s characteristics result from genetic and environmental influences; simple dominant/recessive models describe only some patterns of inheritance.
genetics.example: In a cross Aa × Aa with complete dominance, the genotype probabilities are 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, and 1/4 aa.
genetics.q: For Aa × Aa, what is the probability of genotype aa?
genetics.why: The four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA, and aa.

ecology.title: Ecology & ecosystems
ecology.concept: Energy enters most ecosystems through photosynthesis and moves through feeding relationships. Energy is dissipated at every trophic transfer, while matter cycles between organisms and the environment. Sampling methods must match the organisms and the question being investigated.
ecology.example: Quadrats can estimate abundance of plants. Random placement reduces selection bias; repeated samples show variation and improve the estimate.
ecology.q: Which method best reduces bias in sampling stationary plants?
ecology.why: Random locations avoid deliberately favouring certain parts of the habitat.

evolution.title: Evolution & natural selection
evolution.concept: Populations contain heritable variation. If a trait improves reproductive success in a particular environment, the alleles associated with it may become more frequent over generations. Natural selection acts on existing variation; it does not give individuals traits because they need them.
evolution.example: An antibiotic can leave resistant bacteria more likely to survive and reproduce. The drug does not intentionally train individual bacteria to become resistant.
evolution.q: Natural selection directly depends on differences in…
evolution.why: Heritable traits become more common when their carriers leave more surviving offspring.

homeostasis.title: Homeostasis & human physiology
homeostasis.concept: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within ranges compatible with life. Negative feedback detects deviations and activates responses that oppose them. Regulation often involves coordination among receptors, a processing centre, and effectors.
homeostasis.example: When body temperature rises, increased skin blood flow and sweating can increase heat loss. The response decreases as temperature returns toward its regulated range.
options: Opposes a deviation from a regulated range
homeostasis.why: A negative feedback response counteracts the change that triggered it.

atomic.title: Atomic structure & the periodic table
atomic.concept: Atoms contain a nucleus with protons and usually neutrons, surrounded by electrons. Atomic number counts protons; mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
atomic.example: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons. They have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively. Their chemical similarities follow from their electron arrangements.
atomic.q: Two isotopes of an element differ in their number of…
atomic.why: Their proton numbers identify the same element, while their neutron numbers differ.

bonding.title: Bonding, structure & properties
bonding.concept: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs. Material properties depend on the structure as well as the type of bond, so molecular substances and giant covalent structures behave differently.
bonding.example: Solid sodium chloride has ions fixed in a lattice. When molten, ions can move and carry electric charge.
bonding.q: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
options: It contains freely moving molecules only
bonding.why: Mobile charged ions carry current through the liquid.

moles.title: Chemical quantities & stoichiometry
moles.concept: The mole is a counting unit. Amount in moles equals mass divided by molar mass. A balanced equation gives mole ratios, which allow you to identify the limiting reactant and calculate theoretical product amounts.
moles.example: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 mol of hydrogen require 1 mol of oxygen. If 3 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ are available, oxygen limits the reaction.
moles.q: How many moles are in 18 g of water, with molar mass 18 g mol⁻¹?

energetics.title: Energy changes & reaction rates
energetics.concept: Breaking bonds requires energy and forming bonds releases energy. Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions absorb it. A catalyst changes reaction rate by providing a pathway with lower activation energy.
energetics.example: A catalyst helps a reaction reach equilibrium sooner but does not change the equilibrium position or the overall enthalpy change.
options: Changing the atoms into other elements
energetics.why: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower energy barrier.

acids.title: Acids, bases & equilibria
acids.concept: In aqueous solutions, acids increase hydrogen ion concentration and bases accept protons or produce hydroxide ions. Strong and weak describe extent of ionisation, while concentrated and dilute describe amount per volume. These are different distinctions.
acids.example: A dilute strong acid may contain less hydrogen ion per litre than a sufficiently concentrated weak acid. Use actual concentrations and equilibria when comparing pH.
acids.why: Strength refers to ionisation; concentration refers to amount per volume.

organic.title: Organic chemistry & functional groups
organic.concept: Carbon forms varied chains and rings. A functional group largely determines a compound’s characteristic reactions. Homologous series share a functional group and general chemical patterns, with successive members differing by CH₂.
organic.example: Ethanol has an –OH functional group. Ethanoic acid contains –COOH, so the two compounds have different characteristic reactions.
organic.q: Which functional group identifies a carboxylic acid?

redox.title: Redox & electrochemistry
redox.concept: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. They occur together because electrons transfer between species. Half-equations track atoms and charge separately before being combined.
redox.example: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ represents oxidation. The zinc atom loses two electrons and becomes a positively charged ion.
redox.q: In Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, copper ions are…
redox.why: They gain electrons, which is reduction.

motion.title: Motion & forces
motion.concept: Velocity describes the rate of change of displacement; acceleration describes the rate of change of velocity. The resultant force equals mass times acceleration in the usual constant-mass model. Zero resultant force means constant velocity, which may be zero or non-zero.
motion.example: A 2 kg object accelerating at 3 m s⁻² has a resultant force of 6 N. Forces may still act on an object moving at constant velocity, but they balance.
motion.q: An object moves at constant velocity. Its resultant force is…
options: Equal to its weight in every case
motion.why: There is no acceleration, so the resultant force is zero.

energy.title: Work, energy & power
energy.concept: Work transfers energy when a force acts through a displacement. Energy is conserved across a chosen system and its surroundings. Power is the rate of energy transfer, and efficiency compares useful output with total input.
energy.example: A device transfers 600 J in 3 s. Its average power is 600/3 = 200 W.
energy.q: A machine takes in 100 J and produces 75 J of useful output. Its efficiency is…

waves.title: Waves, light & sound
waves.concept: Waves transfer energy without a net transfer of matter across the whole distance. Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. Reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference describe different behaviours of waves.
waves.example: A wave with frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m travels at 200 m s⁻¹. In a new medium, frequency remains fixed by the source while speed and wavelength can change.
waves.why: v = fλ. The units are s⁻¹ × m = m s⁻¹.

electricity.title: Electric circuits
electricity.concept: Current is the rate of flow of charge. Potential difference measures energy transferred per unit charge. In a series circuit current is the same throughout; parallel branches share the potential difference across their common endpoints.
electricity.example: A 6 Ω resistor with 12 V across it carries 2 A if it obeys Ohm’s law. The power is VI = 24 W.
electricity.q: Two branches connected in parallel have the same…
electricity.why: Each branch connects the same pair of circuit nodes.

thermal.title: Thermal physics & particles
thermal.concept: Temperature relates to the average kinetic energy of particles. Internal energy includes kinetic and potential contributions. A change of state can transfer energy without changing temperature because particle arrangements and interactions change.
thermal.example: When pure ice melts at a fixed pressure, energy can increase internal energy while the temperature remains at the melting point.
thermal.q: During melting at constant pressure, supplied energy mainly…
thermal.why: Energy is associated with the phase change rather than a temperature increase.

fields.title: Fields, gravitation & magnetism
fields.concept: A field describes the force that would act on an appropriate test object at each point. Gravitational fields act on mass; electric fields act on charge. Field lines represent direction and relative strength, rather than physical strings.
fields.example: The gravitational force between point masses varies inversely with the square of their separation. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.
fields.q: If the distance between two point masses doubles, their gravitational force becomes…

nuclear.title: Atomic & nuclear physics
nuclear.concept: Radioactive decay is a random process for an individual unstable nucleus. Half-life describes the time for the expected number of undecayed nuclei in a large sample to halve. Activity measures decays per unit time.
nuclear.example: After three half-lives, the expected undecayed fraction is (1/2)³ = 1/8. This is a statistical prediction for a large sample.
nuclear.q: What fraction remains after two half-lives?

algorithms.title: Algorithms & computational thinking
algorithms.concept: An algorithm is a precise sequence of steps for solving a class of problems. Decomposition breaks a problem into parts; abstraction focuses on relevant details. Trace tables help test a process before it is implemented.
algorithms.example: To find the largest number in a non-empty list, store the first value, compare each remaining value with the stored maximum, and replace the maximum when a larger value appears.
algorithms.q: Why initialise a maximum to the first item instead of zero?
options: Zero is never allowed in programming
algorithms.why: If all values are negative, a maximum initially set to zero may incorrectly stay zero.

programming.title: Programming & data structures
programming.concept: Variables hold values, selection chooses branches, and iteration repeats steps. Functions divide a program into reusable operations. Choose data structures according to the operations needed, and test normal, boundary, and invalid inputs.
programming.example: A function that averages a list must handle the empty-list case before dividing by its length. Checking only a typical positive-number list misses this boundary.
programming.q: Which is a useful boundary test for a list-average function?
options: Only a list of five positive values
programming.why: An empty list exposes a possible division by zero or undefined result.

binary.title: Data representation & computer systems
binary.concept: Binary represents values using powers of two. Text, images, and sound need agreed encodings to be stored digitally. File size depends on representation choices; compression trades off size, processing, and sometimes fidelity.

networks.title: Networks, security & digital responsibility
networks.concept: Networks allow devices to exchange data using protocols. Encryption protects confidentiality; authentication checks identity. A secure system also needs access control, updates, backups, and thoughtful handling of personal data.
networks.example: A password manager can generate distinct passwords so a breach of one website does not automatically expose accounts elsewhere.
networks.q: Which control primarily verifies who a user is?
networks.why: Authentication verifies identity; authorisation decides what that identity may access.

databases.title: Databases & information systems
databases.concept: Relational databases store related data in tables. A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key relates it to another table. Good design reduces unnecessary duplication and supports consistency.
databases.example: A students table stores each student once. An enrolments table connects student IDs to course IDs, supporting many students in many courses.
databases.q: What is the main purpose of a primary key?
databases.why: A primary key is a unique identifier for a table’s records.

text.title: Reading, inference & textual evidence
text.concept: Reading analytically means distinguishing what a text states from what you infer. Support interpretations with carefully selected details. A convincing inference explains how the evidence leads to the claim while allowing for ambiguity.
text.example: If a narrator repeatedly avoids naming a visitor, you might infer anxiety or secrecy. Explain the pattern and consider whether another reading fits the same evidence.
text.q: Which response offers the strongest analytical support?
options: The narrator seems worried because repeated pauses interrupt the greeting
text.why: It identifies a claim, a specific feature, and a link between them.

analysis.title: Language, structure & effect
analysis.concept: Writers make choices about diction, syntax, imagery, voice, and structure. Analysis connects those choices to meaning and context. Naming a technique is a starting point, not an explanation of its effect.
analysis.example: A short sentence after a long descriptive paragraph can interrupt the rhythm and draw attention to a decisive action. The effect depends on the surrounding passage.
analysis.q: After identifying a metaphor, your next step should be to…
options: Explain its meaning and effect in context
Assume every reader feels the same
analysis.why: Analysis explains how the choice shapes meaning in that particular text.

argument.title: Writing an argument
argument.concept: A defensible argument has a focused claim, relevant evidence, and reasoning linking them. Addressing a plausible counterargument can clarify the limits of your position. Paragraph order should guide the reader through a developing line of thought.
argument.example: Claim: the ending is deliberately unresolved. Evidence: the final question is unanswered. Reasoning: the reader must weigh competing interpretations rather than accept a single outcome.
argument.q: Which part explains why evidence supports the claim?
argument.why: Reasoning makes the logical connection between evidence and conclusion.

comparison.title: Comparative literature & perspectives
comparison.concept: A comparison should organise ideas around meaningful similarities and differences. Consider how genre, context, voice, and form affect treatment of a shared concern. Move between works within an argument instead of writing two disconnected summaries.
comparison.example: Compare how two texts depict belonging: one may use an intimate first-person voice, while another uses a fragmented chorus. Discuss what each approach enables the reader to understand.
comparison.q: A strong comparative paragraph is usually organised around…
comparison.why: A common analytical focus lets differences and similarities contribute to the argument.

language.title: Language acquisition & retrieval
language.concept: Language learning combines understanding messages with producing them. Retrieval practice strengthens access to vocabulary, and spaced review revisits words before they are forgotten. Learn words in useful phrases so grammar and meaning stay connected.
language.example: Instead of memorising only a word for transport, practise a sentence about how you travel to school, then change the subject, tense, or reason.
language.q: Which practice most directly tests active recall?
options: Looking at a word list again
Producing a phrase from a meaning prompt
language.why: Producing the phrase requires retrieving it from memory.

listening.title: Listening & speaking strategies
listening.concept: Listen first for purpose and overall meaning, then for specific details. In speaking, communicate a clear idea and build it with reasons or examples. Repairing a misunderstanding is a useful communication skill, not a failure.
listening.example: If you miss a time in an announcement, use the surrounding context and listen for repetition. In conversation, ask the speaker to repeat or clarify rather than guessing silently.
listening.q: If you do not understand an important detail in conversation, the best next step is to…
listening.why: Clarification helps both speakers establish the intended meaning.

grammar.title: Grammar, register & purposeful writing
grammar.concept: Grammar expresses relationships such as time, possibility, cause, and emphasis. Register adapts language to audience and situation. A clear message uses forms appropriate to its purpose, then checks agreement, word order, and consistency.
grammar.example: An email to a friend and a formal request can convey the same basic information, but their greetings, vocabulary, and closing phrases will differ.
grammar.q: Register is most closely related to…
options: Only the length of a text
Language choices for audience and situation
grammar.why: Register reflects the social context and intended reader or listener.

microeconomics.title: Scarcity, markets & elasticity
microeconomics.concept: Scarcity means resources are limited relative to wants, so choices involve opportunity cost. Demand and supply models describe how buyers and sellers respond under stated assumptions. Elasticity measures responsiveness using percentage changes.
microeconomics.example: If quantity demanded falls by 20% after a 10% price rise, the magnitude of price elasticity of demand is 2. Other influences are assumed unchanged.
microeconomics.q: Opportunity cost is the value of…
microeconomics.why: Choosing one option means giving up the best alternative you could otherwise have taken.

macroeconomics.title: Growth, inflation & unemployment
macroeconomics.concept: Macroeconomics studies aggregate outcomes such as output, employment, and the price level. Real measures adjust for price changes. Policy evaluation considers trade-offs, time lags, distribution, and the conditions under which a policy operates.
macroeconomics.example: If nominal output rises 5% while prices rise approximately 3%, real output growth is about 2%; an exact calculation uses 1.05/1.03 − 1.
macroeconomics.q: Why use real GDP when comparing output over time?
options: It ignores population and prices alike
macroeconomics.why: Real GDP aims to separate changes in production from changes in the price level.

trade.title: Trade, development & global connections
trade.concept: Trade allows specialisation but its effects differ among workers, firms, and consumers. Development includes more than income: health, education, distribution, and environmental conditions matter. Compare indicators and examine their limitations.
trade.example: Two countries with similar income per person may have different life expectancy or educational access. A single average cannot describe all lived experiences.
trade.q: Which conclusion is best supported by a rise in GDP per person alone?
options: Average measured output per person has increased
trade.why: The average increases, but the statistic alone does not establish distribution or wider wellbeing.

business.title: Business objectives & stakeholders
business.concept: Businesses combine resources to produce goods and services. Owners, workers, customers, suppliers, communities, and governments may have different objectives. A decision should be evaluated through its costs, benefits, risks, and consequences for stakeholders.
business.example: Automating a production line may lower unit costs and improve consistency, but it requires investment and may affect workers’ roles.
options: Any person or group affected by a business
business.why: Stakeholders include a broader range of affected groups than shareholders.

finance.title: Business finance & accounts
finance.concept: Revenue is income from sales, while profit subtracts relevant costs. Cash flow tracks actual receipts and payments; a profitable business may still run short of cash. Financial statements serve different purposes and must be interpreted in context.
finance.example: A business sells goods on credit for a profit but pays suppliers immediately. It may face a cash shortage before customers pay.
options: Profit always equals cash in the bank
A profitable business can have cash-flow difficulties
A loan is always sales revenue
finance.why: The timing of cash receipts and payments can differ from the recognition of revenue and costs.

accounting.title: Double entry & financial statements
accounting.concept: Every recorded transaction has two corresponding accounting effects. Assets equal liabilities plus equity. The statement of financial position is a snapshot at a date; an income statement reports performance over a period.
accounting.example: Buying equipment for cash increases one asset, equipment, and decreases another asset, cash. Total assets can remain unchanged at the purchase date.
accounting.why: The increase in equipment is balanced by the decrease in cash.

marketing.title: Marketing, operations & human resources
marketing.concept: Marketing identifies customer needs and communicates a suitable offer. Operations organise production and quality; human resources supports recruitment, development, and working relationships. Decisions across these functions affect one another.
marketing.example: A promotion that doubles demand may fail if production capacity cannot increase. Evaluate the whole system, not only the campaign.
marketing.q: Why should a promotion be coordinated with operations?
options: Demand and capacity can affect delivery
marketing.why: The business must be able to fulfil the demand it creates.

history.title: Historical evidence & source evaluation
history.concept: Historical arguments use evidence interpreted in context. Evaluate a source’s origin, purpose, content, and the question it can help answer. A biased source is not automatically useless: its perspective may itself be evidence.
history.example: A political speech may be weak evidence of opponents’ private motives but strong evidence of how the speaker tried to persuade an audience.
history.q: A source with an obvious political purpose is…
options: Useful for some questions but requiring careful evaluation
Only useful if it agrees with your view
history.why: Utility depends on the historical question, the source’s content, and its limitations.

causation.title: Causation, change & historical argument
causation.concept: Historical explanations distinguish long-term conditions, short-term triggers, and decisions by individuals or groups. Causes can interact and vary in significance. A chronology establishes sequence but does not by itself explain why an event occurred.
causation.example: An economic crisis may increase tensions while a political decision triggers a confrontation. Explain the mechanism connecting each factor to the outcome.
causation.q: What turns a list of causes into an explanation?
options: Showing how factors contributed and interacted
Assuming the earliest factor caused everything
causation.why: Explanation identifies causal mechanisms and relationships.

geography.title: Population, settlement & spatial patterns
geography.concept: Geography studies the relationships between people, places, and environments. Population change reflects births, deaths, and migration. Spatial patterns need explanations involving scale, processes, and local context rather than description alone.
geography.example: A city’s population may grow even when births and deaths balance if net migration is positive.
geography.why: Natural increase and net migration together determine the change.

physical.title: Physical geography & landscapes
physical.concept: Landscapes develop through interacting processes such as weathering, erosion, transport, and deposition. Distinguish the breakdown of material in place from its movement. Patterns also depend on geology, climate, time, and human activity.
physical.example: A river deposits more of its carried sediment when flow conditions reduce its capacity to transport that sediment.
physical.q: Which process breaks rock down in place?
physical.why: Weathering breaks down rock where it is; erosion removes material.

climate.title: Climate, resources & sustainability
climate.concept: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes patterns over longer periods. Sustainability requires considering ecological limits, social needs, and economic decisions. Evaluate proposed solutions using evidence, scale, and unintended effects.
climate.example: A single cold day does not disprove a long-term warming trend. Compare appropriately collected records over sufficiently long periods.
climate.q: Why is one day of weather insufficient to establish a climate trend?
climate.why: Short-term variability must be distinguished from a sustained pattern.

fieldwork.title: Fieldwork & research methods
fieldwork.concept: A useful investigation links a focused question to an appropriate sampling strategy and measurement method. Identify independent, dependent, and controlled variables where relevant. Reliability, validity, ethics, and uncertainty all affect the strength of conclusions.
fieldwork.example: To compare river velocity at sites, use a consistent method, repeat measurements, and record conditions. A wider sample supports a more defensible comparison.
fieldwork.q: Repeating measurements mainly helps you assess…
options: Whether a hypothesis must be true
fieldwork.why: Repeated observations reveal variation and help estimate a representative value.

psychology.title: Behaviour, cognition & research design
psychology.concept: Psychology investigates behaviour and mental processes using systematic evidence. Experiments can test causal hypotheses by manipulating variables while controlling alternatives. Correlational studies describe associations but cannot alone establish causation.
psychology.example: A relationship between sleep duration and test scores does not prove sleep is the only cause. Stress, study habits, or health may influence both.
options: That there are no confounding variables
psychology.why: Further evidence is needed to determine causal direction and exclude alternative explanations.

society.title: Culture, identity & social institutions
society.concept: Social research examines how individuals and institutions influence each other. Norms are shared expectations, while values concern what a group regards as important. Avoid treating a community as uniform or confusing an individual example with a population-wide pattern.
society.example: A school rule is a formal norm. Expectations about how students greet one another may be informal norms that vary across groups and situations.
society.q: A social norm is best described as…
society.why: Norms guide what people consider expected or acceptable in a social setting.

politics.title: Power, rights & global politics
politics.concept: Political analysis studies power, legitimacy, institutions, and competing claims. Distinguish a descriptive statement about what happens from a normative claim about what should happen. Evaluate policy through evidence and more than one stakeholder perspective.
politics.example: A policy may improve average outcomes while imposing substantial costs on a minority. Evaluation should identify both the overall effect and its distribution.
options: The vote took place on Monday
politics.why: It expresses a judgment about what ought to be, rather than only describing an observation.

philosophy.title: Philosophical arguments & knowledge
philosophy.concept: An argument offers premises intended to support a conclusion. Validity concerns whether the conclusion follows if the premises are true; soundness also requires true premises. Clarify concepts and test an argument against plausible counterexamples.
philosophy.example: All mammals are animals; whales are mammals; therefore whales are animals. The logical structure supports the conclusion from the premises.
options: Has a conclusion that follows if its premises are true
philosophy.why: Validity concerns the inference; soundness adds the requirement of true premises.

religion.title: Religious traditions & interpretation
religion.concept: Study a tradition through its texts, practices, histories, and the interpretations of its communities. Distinguish an insider account from an external analysis without assuming either perspective is uniform. Use accurate terms and acknowledge diversity within traditions.
religion.example: Two communities sharing a sacred text may interpret or practise aspects differently because of historical, cultural, or theological contexts.
religion.q: Why compare more than one account of a religious tradition?
options: To assume all accounts are identical
religion.why: Multiple accounts help reveal variations in experience and interpretation.

art.title: Visual language & artistic inquiry
art.concept: Artists organise elements such as line, colour, shape, space, and texture to construct meaning. Analyse what is visible before drawing interpretations. Experimentation and reflection connect research with practical decisions.
art.example: Changing a composition’s negative space can alter the balance and emphasis without changing its subject. Make a second version, then compare the effect.
art.why: Negative space is the area surrounding and separating the main forms.

design.title: Design thinking & evaluation
design.concept: A design process begins with an identified need and constraints. Research informs specifications; prototypes test possible solutions. Evaluation compares evidence with success criteria and leads to justified refinements.
design.example: A desk organiser designed for a small surface must be tested for dimensions, stability, accessibility, and usability with the intended user.
options: A vague wish for something nice
A measurable criterion tied to user needs
design.why: Measurable criteria make testing and evaluation meaningful.

music.title: Musical elements & analysis
music.concept: Music combines patterns of rhythm, melody, harmony, texture, timbre, and form. Describe what you hear with precise terms and relate features to their musical context. Performance and composition decisions can test an analytical interpretation.
music.example: A melody repeated with a different accompaniment may feel transformed even if the pitches remain unchanged. Listen for which element changes and explain its effect.
options: The quality or colour of a sound
music.why: Timbre distinguishes sound qualities, such as those of different instruments playing the same pitch.

performance.title: Theatre, dance & performance choices
performance.concept: Performance communicates through bodies, voices, space, timing, and relationships with an audience. Connect choices to an artistic intention. Rehearsal develops a performance through experimentation, feedback, and reflection.
performance.example: A character delivering the same line from opposite sides of a space can change a scene’s power relationships. Compare choices and explain which supports your intention.
options: Link observed effects to specific choices and next steps
performance.why: Reflection uses evidence to improve future performance decisions.

film.title: Film language & storytelling
film.concept: Films construct meaning through framing, camera movement, editing, lighting, mise-en-scène, and sound. Analyse the relationship between a choice and its context rather than assigning every technique one fixed meaning.
film.example: A close-up after a wide shot may shift attention from a setting to a character’s reaction. The accompanying sound and sequence influence its interpretation.
options: The selection and arrangement of shots
film.why: Editing shapes how shots relate in time, space, rhythm, and meaning.

sport.title: Movement, exercise & training
sport.concept: Physical activity depends on coordinated muscular, skeletal, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems. Training adaptations depend on load, recovery, specificity, and individual variation. Use evidence rather than assuming more intensity is always better.
sport.example: A training plan for endurance differs from one focused on explosive strength. Both need appropriate recovery and progression.
sport.q: The principle of specificity means training should…
options: Match the demands of the activity or goal
sport.why: Adaptations are related to the type of training performed.

nutrition.title: Nutrition & food science
nutrition.concept: A balanced diet supplies energy and nutrients in appropriate amounts for individual needs. Food preparation and storage affect safety and quality. Evaluate nutritional claims by considering evidence, portions, and the whole dietary pattern.
nutrition.example: A food described as low fat is not automatically low in sugar or appropriate for every dietary need. Read the wider nutritional information.
nutrition.q: Why is one label claim insufficient to assess a food?
options: Other nutrients, portions, and context also matter
nutrition.why: A single characteristic does not describe the whole food or dietary pattern.

agriculture.title: Agriculture & food systems
agriculture.concept: Agricultural production depends on interactions among soil, water, organisms, climate, technology, and people. Soil management and biodiversity affect long-term productivity. Compare methods using yields, resource use, costs, and environmental effects.
agriculture.example: A crop rotation can interrupt some pest cycles and change nutrient demands. Its suitability depends on the crops, soils, and farming context.
agriculture.q: Why evaluate farming practices over more than one season?
options: Long-term soil and ecosystem effects may differ from immediate yields
agriculture.why: Sustainable productivity involves effects that develop over time.

tourism.title: Tourism & destination management
tourism.concept: Tourism connects visitors, businesses, residents, infrastructure, and environments. Its economic benefits may be unevenly distributed, while environmental and social costs depend on scale and management. Evaluate a destination through multiple stakeholder perspectives.
tourism.example: A busy attraction may create jobs while increasing traffic and pressure on local services. Management can change how benefits and costs are distributed.
tourism.q: Which is a stakeholder in tourism planning?
options: Local residents as well as visitors and businesses
tourism.why: Residents experience many of the effects of tourism and belong in planning discussions.

research.title: Research questions & academic integrity
research.concept: A focused research question is narrow enough to investigate with accessible evidence. Keep track of sources, distinguish quotation from paraphrase, and explain how evidence supports the argument. A bibliography alone does not replace accurate attribution within the work.
research.example: Instead of asking whether all transport is sustainable, investigate a defined route, period, and measure of impact using accessible data.
research.q: A useful research question should be…
options: Focused and answerable with suitable evidence
Guaranteed to prove your first opinion
research.why: A manageable question connects the inquiry to evidence you can actually analyse.

tok.title: Theory of knowledge & justification
tok.concept: TOK examines how knowledge claims are made, supported, and evaluated. Distinguish the claim, the evidence offered, and the assumptions that connect them. Compare perspectives and consider the strengths and limits of methods in different areas of knowledge.
tok.example: A controlled experiment and a historical archive support claims in different ways. Ask which standards of evidence suit the question, rather than assuming one method answers everything.
tok.q: A productive TOK discussion focuses on…
options: How claims are justified and what limits that justification
tok.why: TOK develops critical reflection on knowledge and its justification.

cas.title: CAS planning & reflection
cas.concept: Creativity, activity, and service invite learning through purposeful experience. Set a meaningful intention, consider the needs of others, and reflect on what actually changed. Participation and reflection should be authentic rather than invented to fill a record.
cas.example: After helping organise a community event, reflect on a difficult decision, how you responded, and what you would change in another project.
options: A specific challenge, response, and lesson for next time
A list of hours with no context
cas.why: Specific reflection connects experience with learning and future action.
